newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless drop tied to seasonal factors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless drop tied to seasonal factors.

text.p: A drop in new U.S. jobless claims in the latest week offered yet more evidence of a healthy jobs market but the sharpness of the decline was suspect and probably due to seasonal factors, economists said.

"Jobless claims in general, when you look at a moving average, have been pretty steady over the last several months," said Dana Johnson, managing director and head of research for First Chicago Capital Markets.
New jobless claims fell to 317,000 in the week ended December 7 from a revised 330,000 a week earlier.
Economists polled by Reuters had estimated, on average, that new claims would total 341,000.

Meanwhile, the four-week moving average for new claims slipped to 332,000 in the latest week from 335,000 a week earlier, 335,500 in the week ended November 23 and 336,250 in the week ended November 16.
"Jobless claims in general over the last several months would seem to suggest the job market remains pretty healthy and pretty tight," said Johnson.
But he expressed surprise at the sharpness of the most recent week's drop -- surprise, and some skepticism.

"I'm inclined to withhold judgment because it's often the case that jobless claims tend to get volatile toward the end of the year," said Johnson. "There was no official holiday in that particular week but in general, it's a difficult time to apply seasonal factors."
Johnson said if claims were to stay in the vicinity of 310,000 to 320,000 for several weeks, that could be very important, signalling a stronger labor market than people had imagined.
"But chances are the drop will at least partially reverse itself in the weeks ahead," he concluded.
Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, agreed.
"On the surface, the drop indicates labor market strength," she said. "But it's one week's data and we have to wait and see whether the trend continues."

If initial claims continue to come down slowly but steadily, that would suggest a firmness in the labor market that could aggravate concerns about potential upward pressure on wages, said Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd.

Kahan noted that in the last three weeks for which data were available, the level of continued claims for unemployment insurance has risen, meaning that job creation in the economy is not that robust.
The level of continued claims rose to 2,547,000 in the week ended November 30 from 2,408,000 a week earlier and 2,405,000 in the week ended November 16.

But Kahan said regardless of what the number is, at this time of the year, due to the influences of winter weather as well as holidays, "the seasonally adjusted numbers for claims are somewhat suspect."

"They process fewer claims during Thanksgiving week and fewer are processed during Christmas," said Kahan. "That has less to do with labor market strength than it has to do with who is coming to work in Labor Departments around the country to process claims," he said.
